case.question: Should a professional timer maker develop a home baking timer?
case.source_limits: All companies, sources and observations in this packet are explicitly synthetic evaluation fixtures, not real demand.

sources.excerpt: In this controlled fixture, 24 of 40 participants chose the labelled home-baking timer at the same price. No purchases were collected.
Cedar states its timer tolerates high temperatures. It has not measured consumer demand.

events.text: Compare a home-baking proposition, improved professional distribution, and no expansion; demand and acquisition costs remain unknown.

T1: home bakers forget multiple simultaneous tasks; clearly labelled multi-timers reduce errors, prompting replacement and premium sales. T2: ordinary phone timers suffice; physical timers are purchased for convenient placement, so retail access rather than redesign drives sales. They can coexist; the test compares the proposed dominant purchase drivers.
E1 supports a preference under one equal-price setting, not payment, durable use, or a premium. E2 is only a company claim about heat resistance, not demand.
Search for phone-timer sufficiency and repeat-use barriers. No additional contrary observations in this fixture; lack of a result does not confirm T1.

Propose a bounded, hypothetical randomized choice pilot: identical price and channel, vary multi-task labelling, then measure paid reservation and two-week repeat use. T1 predicts a labelling advantage with fewer forgotten tasks; T2 predicts no material labelling advantage after access is equalized. Sample/cost/thresholds require design validation; do not invest if effects are uncertain. No trial has been run.
No new evidence packet was delivered.
Do not invest in redesign yet. Test the paid-purchase mechanism before commitment. Demand remains unestablished; choose distribution or no expansion if labelling fails to change paid choice.
